title: Night journeys: two passages
paragraphs: PASSAGE A — Lights at the crossing

A youth cycling group wanted to know how visible riders were after sunset on the road beside Taman River. For six evenings, volunteers stood at three fixed crossings and recorded whether each passing bicycle had a front light, a rear light and reflective material. They did not photograph riders or record names. Their purpose was to identify where a safety campaign might be useful, not to accuse individual cyclists.

The first survey suggested that light use was much lower at the riverside crossing than at the other two sites. Yet a school concert had ended nearby that evening, sending many occasional riders along the river road. The group decided that this crowd might not represent the usual traffic. It repeated the riverside count on three ordinary evenings before comparing the locations.

The later counts showed a smaller difference, but rear lights were still less common beside the river. This finding prompted the group to lend rechargeable light sets at a nearby food stall for one week. Most sets were returned, and several riders asked where they could buy their own. The trial was modest, so the group did not claim that lending lights had changed behaviour permanently; it recommended a longer programme with another count one month later.

Every night, Father asked me to turn the small lamp in our bakery window towards the street. Its glow was faint beside the bright sign above the door, and I treated the task as one more delay before we could go home. Father always checked the wick anyway. 'The large sign tells people what this place is,' he said. 'The little light tells them someone is still here.'

During a neighbourhood power cut, the electric sign vanished and the street became unfamiliar. We had already closed the shutters when someone knocked. A delivery rider had fallen at the corner and needed a telephone. He had seen the window lamp from the end of the road and guessed that the bakery was occupied. While Father called for help, I moved the lamp closer to the glass.

After the electricity returned, the lamp looked no brighter than before. Nevertheless, I no longer measured it against the sign. The sign was designed to attract a crowd; the lamp had guided one person who needed us. I still turned it towards the street each evening, but the task no longer felt like a delay. It felt like leaving a quiet answer where a question might appear.
